chunks: And from him (Al-Hadith) from some of our companions, from Al-Fihri, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Al-Mufaddal ibn Umar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), that he said:
"Whoever mounts a riding animal (camel), then falls from it and dies, enters Hell."

The explanation (waajh) in this report is what Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Babawayh (may God have mercy on him) mentioned, that it was the custom of the Arabs: when they wanted to dismount, they threw themselves from the riding animal without holding onto anything on it.
So the meaning of these two reports is that if he has a means (face/wealth) by which he can pay his debt from it,
as for one who does not have that, he should not borrow for Hajj.
This is indicated by what he narrated:
ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to borrow money for Hajj if you cannot repay it?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the permissibility of borrowing for Hajj by resolving an apparent contradiction regarding the fate of those who die from their mounts. Ibn Babawayh explains that the 'falling' refers to the reckless Arab custom of dismounting without securing the animal, implying that death due to debt-induced recklessness leads to Hell, whereas those with the means to repay are exempt. Thus, the ruling hinges on the borrower's ability to settle the debt, ensuring that Hajj does not become a burden of insolvency.
